source.title: Brainformers: Trading Simplicity for Efficiency
source.authors: Yan-Qi Zhou; Nan Du; Yan-Ping Huang; Dai-Yi Peng; Chang Lan; Da Huang; Siamak Shakeri; David R. So; Andrew M. Dai; Yifeng Lu; Zhi-Feng Chen; Quoc V. Le; Claire Cui; J. Laudon; J. Dean

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study ablates Brainformer block architecture and reports how layer ordering and layer-type composition affect model quality, a conceptual test of architecture sensitivity.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work and discusses compute-efficient scaling, but does not fit or test power laws or optimize parameter-token allocation. Its perplexity comparisons across Brainformer and baseline models do not establish those claims. Downstream benchmark comparisons are not tests of downstream predictability as defined here.
record.test_reason: Only the Section 6.2 block ablation bears on a version. It reports qualitatively that reordering sub-layers within a fixed block barely changes quality, which concerns V4 (architecture details at fixed parameter count). The rest of the paper compares its searched architecture with baselines. It fits no scaling law and makes no allocation or extrapolation test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only the ablation. The main conclusion is that the evolutionary-searched heterogeneous Brainformer block beats GLaM and Primer. It gives up to 2x faster convergence, 5x faster step time and about 3% higher SuperGLUE at similar activated parameters. The authors also propose fixed-training-time comparisons. Secondarily, the layer-type ratio matters while layer order matters little.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture-search and ablation study, not a reproduction of the original scaling-law methods. It tests heterogeneous layer composition and ordering rather than fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports sensitivity to layer-type ratios but relatively little sensitivity to layer ordering.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 202, 2023
record.problems: The architecture-ablation findings are qualitative: no numerical outcomes, uncertainty estimates, or details of the tested replacements are reported.

untested.parts: Depth versus width and aspect ratio at fixed parameter count; a wide range of shapes; dense models; any numerical loss differences.
No power-law fit. Figure 1 shows perplexity against log activated parameters for three MoE scales only, with no fit.
Not tested. The fixed-wall-clock search is cited as resonating with Chinchilla but does not measure an optimal allocation.
Downstream scores compare architectures at two scales; predictability from scale or loss is not tested.

missing.what: Architectures at roughly similar activated parameters differ in eval perplexity: 100M32E GLaM 2.73, Search-w-Top2 2.67, Brainformer-1 2.57. These are the study's own searched models against baselines, with unmatched parameter counts and partly different routing. They are weak, confounded evidence on V4 and should not count as a clean test.

Changing only the gating function at the same 8B64E architecture and parameters lowers perplexity from 2.12 (GLaM top-2) to 2.03 (expert-based gating). This is a routing change, not a depth or width change.

record.verdict_notes: An architecture-search paper on MoE models. Its link to scaling-law versions is weak. The V4 support rests on a single qualitative sentence with no numbers, and r2 should not count as a challenge. The record's uncertainty_reported 'y' applies only to Table 3 perplexities, not to the ablation. The 'near-perfect log-scale scaling' remark (Fig. 1) covers three points with no fit, so it cannot bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test across parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
The study does not find loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations across fixed compute budgets.
The ablation does not report controlled fixed-parameter-count comparisons or systematic tests of depth and width across a wide range.
The study is on NLP language models and does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes.
Downstream tasks are compared across architectures, but the study does not test whether task performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation are compared across fitting choices, and no bending of scaling curves is tested.

rows.subject: Brainformer block architecture
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the ordering of sub-layers by swapping layer positions.
rows.value: The authors report that swapping any two layers would not affect performance much.
rows.note: The statement concerns sensitivity to layer order; no numerical ablation result is provided.
rows.check: Linked correctly. Reordering keeps layer types and parameter count fixed, so this is a fixed-size architecture change. The evidence is qualitative only: no perplexity numbers, no stated scale or set of permutations. The subject is a sparse MoE Brainformer block, not a dense transformer.

rows.subject: Brainformer block architecture
rows.operation_detail: Ablated layer-type composition by replacing a layer with a different layer.
rows.value: The authors report that the ratio of layer types is critical to quality and that replacing a layer with a different type degrades quality.
rows.note: The paper gives no numerical magnitude for the degradation.
rows.check: The state was wrongly set to reversed. Replacing one layer type with another (e.g. MoE with dense FFN) likely changes total and activated parameters, so it is not a fixed-parameter shape change. The size of the degradation is not given, so it cannot show more than a 'slight' effect. This cannot challenge V4.

relationships.condition: Reordering sub-layers within a fixed Brainformer MoE block (fixed layer types and parameter count)
relationships.reason: The authors state swapping any two layers would not affect performance much (r1). The claim is qualitative, with no numbers.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported that swapping any two sub-layers within the fixed block would have little effect on performance.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
